title: Zen centers in the West
hook: Zen centers founded by Japanese, Korean and Vietnamese teachers

segments.voice: Yesterday, communities of practice: Anuruddha and his friends, mixing like milk and water. Your line was living together. Did you set out the seats first, or clean up last? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-eight.

A row of shoes by a door on a city street. Sneakers, work boots, a pair of heels, lined up neatly on a wooden rack. Upstairs, in a room that used to be an office, people in dark clothes sit facing a white wall. A wooden board is struck outside, then a bell inside. No one moves. Not long ago some of them were on the subway. Rooms like this exist in cities and farmhouses across Europe and the Americas, and this one, like others, traces back to a teacher who crossed an ocean. Today: Zen centers in the West.
screen: `A ROW OF SHOES.` → `FACING A WHITE WALL.` → `A TEACHER WHO CROSSED AN OCEAN.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Tradition traces the word Zen back through the Chinese Chan to the Sanskrit dhyana, meditation. So the name itself has already traveled: from India to China, and from China to Korea, Japan and Vietnam, where it is called Seon and Thien. Second, the teachers. Western Zen centers were founded by teachers from more than one of those homes. From Japan came teachers such as Shunryu Suzuki, who helped found the San Francisco Zen Center. From Korea came Seung Sahn, whose students formed the Kwan Um School. From Vietnam came Thich Nhat Hanh, whom we met at the start of this week. Each brought the chants, forms and flavor of his own country, so a Japanese-style zendo and a Korean-style dharma room don't feel quite the same. Third, what they faced. These teachers arrived far from home, teaching students who knew little of Buddhist culture. Some Western students wanted meditation without the bowing and chanting. The teachers had to decide what to keep, what to translate and what to let go, and they didn't all decide the same way. Fourth, the week behind us. We started with engaged Buddhism and the stretcher, went to hospices and prisons, to Taiwan's temples, schools and relief teams, to the family altar, and to people living together. Zen in the West closes the week the way it began: practice carried a long way from where it started, and still recognizably itself.
screen: `DHYANA, CHAN, SEON, THIEN, ZEN.` · `TEACHERS FROM JAPAN, KOREA, VIETNAM.` · `WHAT TO KEEP, WHAT TO TRANSLATE.` · `A WEEK OF PRACTICE ON THE MOVE.` · then, large: `FAR FROM HOME.`

segments.voice: Here is a way to try it, if you'd like, in the style of a zendo. Sit upright, hands resting in your lap, eyes lowered, facing a plain wall if there's one near you. Let your breath be ordinary. Count each out-breath, one to ten, and start again whenever you lose count. That's all. Teachers from Japan, Korea and Vietnam each taught some version of this, far from home, to people who had never sat before. When the bell rings, you'll have done what they came to share. The bell holds the time.
Zen centers in the West. Meditation halls in Europe and the Americas founded by teachers from Japan, Korea and Vietnam, each carrying the forms of home. Today's word.
screen: `ZEN CENTERS IN THE WEST — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: far from home. Today, look up one Zen center or Buddhist temple near you, and notice which country its teachers came from. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Western Zen centers hold daily or weekly sitting periods, often facing a wall or the center of the room, with chanting, bowing and talks in the style of the Japanese, Korean or Vietnamese lineage that founded them.
